text: Kobe Bean Bryant (/ˈkoʊbi/ KOH-bee; August 23, 1978 – January 26, 2020) was an American professional basketball player who played as a shooting guard and spent his entire 20-year career with the Los Angeles Lakers in the National Basketball Association (NBA). Widely regarded as one of the greatest and most influential basketball players in history, Bryant won five NBA championships, was an 18-time All-Star, four-time All-Star MVP, 15-time member of the All-NBA Team, 12-time member of the All-Defensive Team, the 2008 NBA Most Valuable Player (MVP), two-time NBA Finals MVP, and two-time scoring champion. He ranks fourth in league all-time regular season and postseason scoring. Bryant was posthumously named to the NBA 75th Anniversary Team in 2021 and was a two-time inductee to the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame, as a player in 2020 and as a member of the 2008 U.S. Olympic team in 2025. The son of NBA player Joe Bryant, Bryant was born in Philadelphia and partly raised in Italy. Recognized as the top American high school basketball player while at Lower Merion High School in the Philadelphia suburb of Ardmore, Bryant declared for the 1996 NBA draft and was selected by the Charlotte Hornets with the 13th pick; he was then traded to the Lakers. As a rookie, Bryant earned a reputation as a high-flyer by winning the 1997 Slam Dunk Contest and was named an All-Star by his second season. Despite his contentious relationship with teammate Shaquille O'Neal, the pair led the Lakers to three consecutive NBA championships from 2000 to 2002. In 2003, Bryant was charged with sexual assault. Charges were dropped after the accuser refused to testify, and a lawsuit was settled out of court, with Bryant issuing an apology and admitting to a sexual encounter he maintained was consensual. After the Lakers lost the 2004 NBA Finals, O'Neal was traded and Bryant became the franchise's cornerstone. He led the NBA in scoring in the 2005–06 and 2006–07 seasons. On January 22, 2006, Bryant scored a career-high 81 points, the second most scored in a single NBA game behind Wilt Chamberlain's 100-point game. Bryant led the team to championships in 2009 and 2010, and was named NBA Finals MVP both times. He continued to be among the league's premier players through the 2012–13 season when he suffered a torn achilles tendon. The last years of his playing career were hampered by injuries and limited playing time. Bryant retired after the 2015–16 season, capping off his illustrious career with a 60-point performance in his final NBA game. In 2017, the Lakers retired both his Nos. 8 and 24, making Bryant the only player in NBA history to have multiple numbers retired by the same franchise. The all-time leading scorer in Lakers history, Bryant was the first guard in NBA history to play 20 seasons. His 18 All-Star designations are the third most ever, and his four NBA All-Star Game MVP Awards are tied with Bob Pettit for the most in history. Bryant gave himself the nickname Black Mamba in the mid-2000s, and the epithet became widely adopted by the public. He won gold medals on the 2008 and 2012 U.S. Olympic teams. In 2018, Bryant won the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film for Dear Basketball (2017), becoming the only person to win both an Olympic gold medal and an Oscar. In January 2020, Bryant and his 13-year-old daughter Gianna were among nine people who died in a helicopter crash in Calabasas, California. A number of tributes and memorials followed, and the All-Star Game MVP Award was renamed in Bryant's honor. Kobe Bean Bryant was born on August 23, 1978, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. His mother, Pam Bryant (née Cox), is the sister of basketball player Chubby Cox, and his father, Joe Bryant, played eight seasons in the NBA. He has two older sisters: Sharia and Shaya. His father named him after the Kobe beef from Japan, which he saw on a restaurant menu, whereas his middle name, Bean, was derived from his father's nickname "Jellybean". Bryant's family was Catholic and he was brought up with this faith. Bryant started playing basketball at the age of three, and the Lakers were his favorite team when he was growing up. When Bryant was six, his father retired from the NBA and moved his family to Rieti in Italy to continue playing professional basketball. After two years, they moved first to Reggio Calabria, then to Pistoia and Reggio Emilia. Kobe became accustomed to his new lifestyle and learned to speak fluent Italian. He was especially fond of Reggio Emilia, which Kobe considered a loving place and where some of his best childhood memories were made. Kobe began to play basketball seriously while living in Reggio Emilia. His grandfather mailed him videos of NBA games for him to study. Another source of inspiration was animated European films about sports, from which Kobe learned more about basketball. From 1987 to 1989, his father played for Olimpia Basket Pistoia where he paired with former Detroit Pistons player Leon Douglas. Kobe worked at the games as a ball and mop boy and practiced shooting at halftime. Douglas said, "At every one of our games at halftime, it was the Kobe show. He'd get out there and get his shot up. We'd come out of the locker room at halftime and have to chase him off the court". Bryant also learned to play soccer, and his favorite soccer team was A.C. Milan. During summers, Bryant returned to the United States to play in a basketball summer league. When he was 13, Bryant and his family moved back to Philadelphia, where he enrolled in the eighth grade at Bala Cynwyd Middle School. Bryant earned national recognition during a spectacular high-school career at Lower Merion High School in Ardmore, located in the Philadelphia suburb of Lower Merion. He played on the varsity basketball team as a freshman. Bryant became the first freshman in decades to start for Lower Merion's varsity team, but the team finished with a 4–20 record. The following three years, the Aces compiled a 77–13 record, with Bryant playing all five positions. During his junior year, Bryant averaged 31.1 points, 10.4 rebounds, 5.2 assists, 3.8 blocks and 2.3 steals and was named Pennsylvania Player of the Year while also earning a fourth-team Parade All-American nomination, attracting attention from college recruiters in the process. Duke, Michigan, North Carolina and Villanova were at the top of his list. However, after high schooler Kevin Garnett went in the first round of the 1995 NBA draft, Bryant also began contemplating going directly to the pros. At Adidas ABCD Camp, Bryant earned the 1995 senior MVP award while playing alongside future NBA teammate Lamar Odom. While in high school, then 76ers coach John Lucas invited Bryant to work out and scrimmage with the team, where he played one-on-one with Jerry Stackhouse. As a senior, Bryant led the Aces to their first state championship in 53 years. During the run, he averaged 30.8 points, 12 rebounds, 6.5 assists, 4 steals, and 3.8 blocked shots in leading the Aces to a 31–3 record. Bryant finished his high-school career as Southeastern Pennsylvania's all-time leading scorer at 2,883 points, surpassing both Wilt Chamberlain and Lionel Simmons. Bryant received several awards for his outstanding performance during his senior year at Lower Merion. These included being named Naismith High School Player of the Year, Gatorade Men's National Basketball Player of the Year, a McDonald's All-American, a first-team Parade All-American and a USA Today All-USA First Team player. Bryant's varsity coach, Greg Downer, commented that he was "a complete player who dominates" and praised his work ethic, even as the team's top player. In 1996, Bryant took R&B singer Brandy to her Hollywood High senior prom. Ultimately, the 17-year-old Bryant decided to go directly into the NBA, becoming only the sixth player in NBA history to do so. His news was met with a significant publicity at a time when prep-to-pro NBA players were not very common (Kevin Garnett being the only exception in 20 years). His basketball skills and SAT score of 1080 would have ensured admission to any college Bryant chose, but he did not officially visit any campuses. In 2012, Bryant was honored as one of the 35 Greatest McDonald's All-Americans for his high school play as well as his later accomplishments. Before the 1996 NBA draft, Bryant had worked out in Los Angeles, where he scrimmaged against former Lakers players Larry Drew and Michael Cooper and, according to then-Laker general manager Jerry West, "marched over these people". The Lakers were looking to trade their starting center Vlade Divac for a player's draft rights to free up salary cap space to make an offer to free-agent center Shaquille O'Neal. Bill Branch, the Charlotte Hornets' head scout at the time, said that the Hornets agreed to trade their No. 13 pick to the Lakers the day before the draft. Before the trade agreement, the Hornets never considered drafting Bryant. During the draft, the Lakers told the Hornets whom to select minutes before the pick was made. Bryant was the first guard drafted directly out of high school. After the draft, the trade was put in jeopardy when Divac threatened to retire rather than be traded from Los Angeles. However, on June 30, Divac relented on his threat and the trade was made final on July 9, 1996, when the league's off-season moratorium ended. Since Bryant was still 17 at the time, his parents had to co-sign his contract with the Lakers until Bryant was able to sign his own when he turned 18 before the season began. Bryant signed a three-year rookie contract totaling $3.5 million. Bryant debuted in the Summer Pro League in Long Beach, California, scoring 25 points in front of a standing-room-only crowd. Defenders struggled to get in front of him, and his performance excited West and Lakers coach Del Harris. Bryant scored 36 points in the finale and finished with averages of 24.5 points and 5.3 rebounds in four games. As a rookie in 1996–97, Bryant mostly came off the bench behind guards Eddie Jones and Nick Van Exel. At the time, he was the second-youngest player ever to play in an NBA game (18 years, 72 days) and also became the youngest NBA starter (18 years, 158 days). Initially, Bryant played limited minutes, but as the season continued, he began to see some more playing time. By the end of the season, Bryant averaged 15.5 minutes a game. During the All-Star weekend, he participated in the Rookie Challenge and won the 1997 Slam Dunk Contest, becoming the youngest dunk champion at the age of 18. Bryant's performance throughout the year earned him a spot on the NBA All-Rookie Second Team with fellow bench teammate Travis Knight. The Lakers advanced to the Western Conference semifinals in the playoffs against the Utah Jazz, when Bryant was pressed into a lead role at the end of Game 5. Byron Scott missed the game with a sprained wrist, Robert Horry was ejected for fighting with Utah's Jeff Hornacek, and Shaquille O'Neal fouled out with 1:46 remaining in the fourth quarter. Bryant shot four air balls at the end of the game; the Jazz won 98–93 in overtime to eliminate the Lakers 4–1. He first missed a game-winning two-point jump shot in the fourth quarter, and then misfired three three-point field goals in overtime, including two tying shots in the final minute. O'Neal commented that "[Bryant] was the only guy who had the guts at the time to take shots like that". In Bryant's second season, he received more playing time and began to show more of his abilities as a talented young guard. As a result, Bryant's point averages more than doubled, from 7.6 to 15.4 points per game. He would see an increase in minutes when the Lakers "played small", which would feature Bryant playing small forward alongside the guards he would usually back up. Bryant was the runner-up for the NBA's Sixth Man of the Year Award, and through fan voting, he also became the youngest NBA All-Star starter in NBA history. Bryant was joined by teammates O'Neal, Van Exel, and Jones, making it the first time since 1983 that four players on the same team were selected to play in the same All-Star Game. Bryant's 15.4 points per game was the highest of any non-starter in the season. The 1998–99 season marked Bryant's emergence as a premier guard in the league. With starting guards Van Exel and Jones traded, Bryant started every game for the lockout-shortened 50-game season. During the season, he signed a six-year contract extension worth $70 million. This kept Bryant with the Lakers until the end of the 2003–04 season. Even at an early stage of his career, sportswriters were comparing Bryant's skills to those of Michael Jordan and Magic Johnson. However, the playoff results were no better as the Lakers were swept by the San Antonio Spurs in the Western Conference Semifinals. Bryant's fortunes improved when Phil Jackson took over as coach of the Lakers in 1999. After years of steady improvement, Bryant became one of the premier shooting guards in the league, earning appearances in the league's All-NBA, All-Star, and All-Defensive teams. The Lakers became championship contenders behind the center-guard combination of Bryant and O'Neal. Jackson utilized the triangle offense that he implemented to win six championships with the Chicago Bulls; this offense would help both Bryant and O'Neal rise to the elite class of the NBA. Three championships were won consecutively in 2000, 2001, and 2002, further cementing this view. Bryant was sidelined for six weeks prior to the start of the 1999–2000 season due to a hand injury that he had incurred during a preseason game against the Washington Wizards. When Bryant was back and playing over 38 minutes a game, he had an increase in all statistical categories during the 1999–2000 season. This included leading the team in assists per game and steals per game. The duo of O'Neal and Bryant backed with a strong bench led to the Lakers winning 67 games, tied for fifth-most in NBA history. This followed with O'Neal winning the MVP and Bryant being named to the All-NBA Second Team and All-NBA Defensive Team for the first time in his career (the youngest player to receive All-Defensive honors). While playing second fiddle to O'Neal in the playoffs, Bryant had some clutch performances, including a 25-point, 11-rebound, seven-assist, four-block game in Game 7 of the Western Conference Finals against the Portland Trail Blazers. He also threw an alley-oop pass to O'Neal to clinch the game and the series. In the 2000 Finals, against the Indiana Pacers, Bryant injured his ankle in the second quarter of Game 2 after landing on the Pacers' Jalen Rose's foot. Rose later admitted he placed his foot under Bryant intentionally. Bryant did not return to the game, and he also missed Game 3 due to the injury. In Game 4, Bryant scored 22 points in the second half and led the team to an overtime victory as O'Neal fouled out of the game. Bryant scored the winning shot to put the Lakers ahead 120–118. With a 116–111 victory in Game 6, the Lakers won their first championship since 1988. Statistically, the 2000–01 season saw Bryant perform similarly to the previous year, but he averaged six more points per game (28.5). It was also the year when disagreements between Bryant and O'Neal began to surface. Once again, Bryant led the team in assists, with five per game. However, the Lakers only won 56 games, an 11-game drop-off from the previous year. The team responded by going 15–1 in the playoffs. They easily swept the Portland Trail Blazers in the first round. In the semifinals round, the Lakers swept the Sacramento Kings. In Game 4 against the Kings, Bryant recorded 48 points, 16 rebounds, and three assists in a 119–1.

In Game 4, Bryant scored 22 points in the second half and led the team to an overtime victory as O'Neal fouled out, with Bryant scoring the winning shot to put the Lakers ahead 120–118. With a 116–111 victory in Game 6, the Lakers won their first championship since 1988. Statistically, the 2000–01 season saw Bryant perform similarly to the previous year, averaging six more points per game (28.5), and he again led the team in assists with five per game. However, the Lakers only won 56 games, an 11-game drop-off from the prior year. The team responded by going 15–1 in the playoffs, sweeping the Portland Trail Blazers in the first round and the Sacramento Kings in the semifinals, with Bryant recording 48 points, 16 rebounds, and three assists in a 119–113 series-clinching victory in Game 4. They swept the San Antonio Spurs in the Conference Finals to reach the Finals, where they lost their first game to the Philadelphia 76ers in overtime but won the next four games to bring their second championship to Los Angeles in as many seasons. During the playoffs, Bryant played heavy minutes, raising his stats to 29.4 points, 7.3 rebounds, and 6.1 assists per game, and teammate O'Neal declared Bryant the best player in the league. Bryant made the All-NBA Second Team and All-NBA Defensive Team for the second year in a row and was voted to start in the NBA All-Star Game for the third year in a row (no game in 1999). In the 2001–02 season, Bryant played 80 games for the first time in his career. On January 14, 2002, he recorded a then-career-high 56 points with five rebounds and four assists in a 120–81 victory over the Memphis Grizzlies. He averaged 25.2 points, 5.5 rebounds, and 5.5 assists per game, had a career-high 46.9% shooting, and led the team in assists. Bryant won his first All-Star MVP trophy after a 31-point performance in Philadelphia, despite being loudly booed by fans due to a prior comment about cutting fans' hearts out. He was named to the All-NBA First Team for the first time and made the All-NBA Defensive Team again. The Lakers won 58 games and finished second in the Pacific Division behind the Sacramento Kings. Bryant was suspended for one game after punching Reggie Miller of the Indiana Pacers following a March 1, 2002, victory. The road to the 2002 Finals was tougher than the previous year; the Lakers swept the Blazers and defeated the Spurs 4–1 in the first two playoff rounds, but lacked home-court advantage against the Sacramento Kings, resulting in a seven-game series—the first time since the 2000 Western Conference Finals. The Lakers beat their division rivals and made their third consecutive NBA Finals appearance. In the 2002 Finals against the New Jersey Nets, Bryant averaged 26.8 points, 51.4% shooting, 5.8 rebounds, and 5.3 assists per game, scoring a quarter of the team's points. At age 23, he became the youngest player to win three championships. His performance in the fourth quarter of games, especially in the last two playoff rounds, was notable and cemented his reputation as a "clutch player." In the first game of the 2002–03 season, Bryant recorded 27 points, 10 rebounds, five assists, and four steals in an 87–82 loss to the Spurs. On November 1, he recorded a triple-double of 33 points, 15 rebounds, and 12 assists in a 108–93 victory over the Clippers. On January 7, 2003, he set an NBA record for three-pointers in a game by making 12 against the Seattle SuperSonics. He averaged 30 points per game and posted 40 or more points in nine consecutive games, averaging 40.6 in February. He averaged 6.9 rebounds, 5.9 assists, and 2.2 steals per game, all career-highs. He was voted to both the All-NBA and All-Defensive First Teams and came in third for the MVP award. After finishing 50–32, the Lakers lost in the Western Conference semifinals in six games to the San Antonio Spurs. The following season, the Lakers acquired Karl Malone and Gary Payton. Bryant was arrested for sexual assault before the season began, missing some games due to court appearances or attending court earlier and playing later. In the final game of the regular season, the Lakers played the Portland Trail Blazers; Bryant made two buzzer-beaters to win the game and the Pacific Division title. With 1.1 seconds left in the fourth quarter, he made a three-pointer to send it to overtime, and in the second overtime, he made another three-pointer as time expired to narrowly win 105–104. With a starting lineup of O'Neal, Malone, Payton, and Bryant, the Lakers reached the 2004 Finals but were upset in five games by the Detroit Pistons, who won their first championship since 1990. In that series, Bryant averaged 22.6 points per game and 4.4 assists while shooting 35.1% from the field. Jackson's contract as coach was not renewed, and Rudy Tomjanovich took over. O'Neal was traded to the Miami Heat for Lamar Odom, Caron Butler, and Brian Grant. The next day, Bryant declined a six-year, $100 million offer to sign with the Clippers and re-signed with the Lakers on a seven-year, $136.4 million contract. During the 2004–05 season, Bryant was heavily criticized, with Jackson's book The Last Season: A Team in Search of Its Soul containing criticisms of Bryant, including calling him "un-coachable." Midway through the season, Tomjanovich resigned due to health problems and exhaustion, and Frank Hamblen took over as interim coach. Bryant was the league's second-leading scorer at 27.6 points per game, but the Lakers went 34–48 and missed the playoffs for the first time in over a decade. Bryant did not make the All-Defensive Team and was demoted to the All-NBA Third Team. He also engaged in public feuds with Malone and Ray Allen. In the 2005–06 season, Jackson returned as coach, and Bryant endorsed the move, working well together and leading the Lakers back into the playoffs. This marked Bryant's finest statistical season, with 62 points in three quarters against the Dallas Mavericks on December 20, 2005, where he personally outscored the entire Mavericks team 62–61, the only time a player has done this through three quarters since the shot clock began. On January 16, 2006, Bryant and O'Neal engaged in handshakes and hugs before a game against the Miami Heat, signaling a change in their feud. At the 2006 NBA All-Star Game, they were seen laughing together. On January 22, 2006, Bryant scored a career-high 81 points in a 122–104 victory over the Toronto Raptors, breaking Elgin Baylor's franchise record of 71 and becoming the second-highest scorer in NBA history, surpassed only by Chamberlain's 100-point game in 1962. While Chamberlain was fed repeatedly by teammates in a blowout, Bryant created his own shots mostly from the outside, with the Lakers trailing at halftime by 14 and not pulling away until the fourth quarter. Chamberlain accounted for 59% of his team's points in a 169–147 win, compared to Bryant scoring 66% of the Lakers' 122 points. That month, Bryant became the first player since 1964 to score 45 points or more in four consecutive games, joining Chamberlain and Baylor. For January, Bryant averaged 43.4 points per game, the eighth-highest single-month average in NBA history and the highest for any player other than Chamberlain. By the end of the 2005–06 season, Bryant set Lakers single-season records for most 40-point games (27) and most points scored (2,832). He won the scoring title for the first time, averaging 35.4 points per game, becoming just the fifth player in league history to average at least 35 in a season. He finished fourth in MVP voting with 22 first-place votes, second only to Steve Nash. Later in the season, Bryant changed his jersey number from 8 to 24 at the start of the 2006–07 season. His first high-school number was 24, before switching to 33. He wanted 24 as a rookie but it was unavailable due to George McCloud, and 33 was retired by Kareem Abdul-Jabbar. He wore 143 at the Adidas ABCD camp and chose 8 by adding those numbers. In the first round of the playoffs, the Lakers reached a 3–1 series lead over the Phoenix Suns, with Bryant scoring overtime-forcing and game-winning shots in Game 4. They came within six seconds of eliminating the Suns in Game 6 but lost 126–118 in overtime. Despite scoring 50 points on 20 of 35 shooting in the Game 6 loss, Bryant was criticized for only taking three shots in the second half of the 121–90 Game 7 loss. In the 2006–07 season, Bryant made his ninth All-Star Game appearance and on February 18 earned his second All-Star Game MVP with 31 points, six assists, and six steals. He had on-court incidents: on January 28, he struck San Antonio guard Manu Ginóbili in the face with his elbow while attempting to draw contact, leading to a one-game suspension for an "unnatural motion" in swinging his arm backward; on March 6, he repeated the motion, striking Minnesota guard Marko Jarić, resulting in a second one-game suspension; in his first game back on March 9, he elbowed Kyle Korver in the face, retroactively classified as a Type 1 flagrant foul. On March 16, Bryant scored a season-high 65 points in a home win against the Portland Trail Blazers, ending a seven-game losing streak—this was the second-best scoring performance of his 11-year career. The next game, he scored 50 points against the Timberwolves, and then 60 points in a road win against the Memphis Grizzlies, becoming the second Laker to score three straight 50-plus point games, a feat not seen since Jordan in 1987. The only other Laker to do so was Baylor, who scored 50+ in three consecutive games in December 1962. The next day, in a game against the New Orleans/Oklahoma City Hornets, Bryant scored 50 points, making him the second player in NBA history to have four straight 50-point games, behind Chamberlain, who achieved it twice with streaks of five and seven. Bryant finished the year with 10 50-plus point games, surpassed only by Chamberlain. He won his second straight scoring title. Throughout the 2006–07 season, Bryant's jersey became the top-selling NBA jersey in the United States and China, with journalists attributing the sales boost to his new number and All-Star performance. In the 2007 NBA playoffs, the Lakers were eliminated in the first round by the Phoenix Suns, 4–1. On May 27, 2007, ESPN reported Bryant stated he wanted to be traded if Jerry West did not return with full authority. He later confirmed his desire for West's return but denied wanting to be traded if that did not happen. Three days later, on Stephen A. Smith's radio program, Bryant expressed anger over a Lakers "insider" claiming he was responsible for O'Neal's departure and publicly stated, "I want to be traded." Three hours later, he reconsidered after speaking with head coach Jackson and backed off the trade request. He was later shown in an infamous amateur video saying center Andrew Bynum should have been traded for All-Star Jason Kidd. On December 23, 2007, Bryant became the youngest player (29 years, 122 days) to reach 20,000 points, scoring 39 points with 11 rebounds and eight assists against the New York Knicks in Madison Square Garden. This record has since been broken by LeBron James. On March 28, Bryant scored a season-high 53 points with 10 rebounds in a loss to the Memphis Grizzlies. Despite an injury to his shooting hand's small finger—described as a complete tear of the radial collateral ligament, an avulsion fracture, and a volar plate injury at the MCP joint—occurring in a game on February 5, 2008, Bryant played all 82 games of the regular season instead of opting for surgery. He stated, "I would prefer to delay any surgical procedure until after our Lakers season and this summer's Olympic Games. But, this is an injury that myself [sic] and the Lakers' medical staff will just have to continue to monitor on a day-to-day basis." Aided by the trade for All-Star Pau Gasol, Bryant led the Lakers to a West-leading 57–25 record. The Lakers swept the Denver Nuggets in the first round, and on May 6, 2008, Bryant was officially announced as the league MVP. He said, "It's been a long ride. I'm very proud to represent this organization, to represent this city."

Bryant recorded 53 points and 10 rebounds in a loss to the Memphis Grizzlies. Despite suffering a complete tear of the radial collateral ligament, an avulsion fracture, and a volar plate injury at the MCP joint in his right pinkie on February 5, 2008, he played all 82 regular-season games instead of undergoing surgery, stating he preferred to delay any procedure until after the Lakers' season and the 2008 Olympics, and that he and the Lakers' medical staff would continue to monitor the injury daily. Aided by the trade for All-Star Pau Gasol, Bryant led the Lakers to a 57–25 record, finishing first in the Western Conference. The Lakers swept the Denver Nuggets in the first round, and on May 6, 2008, Bryant was officially named league MVP; he said, "It's been a long ride. I'm very proud to represent this organization, to represent this city." West, who brought Bryant to the Lakers, was present at the press conference where Bryant received the MVP trophy from NBA commissioner David Stern, who stated, "Kobe deserved it. He's had just another great season. Doesn't surprise me one bit." Bryant was the only unanimous selection to the All-NBA team for the third consecutive season and sixth time in his career, and he earned his eighth All-Defensive First Team selection with 52 points, including 24 first-place nods. The Lakers finished the 2007–08 season with a 57–25 record, setting up a first-round matchup against the Nuggets. In Game 1, Bryant scored 18 of his 32 points in the final eight minutes to keep the Lakers ahead. Denver became the first 50-win team to be swept in the first round since the Memphis Grizzlies were eliminated by the San Antonio Spurs in 2004. In the next round against the Utah Jazz, Bryant scored 38 points in Game 1. The Lakers won Game 2 but lost Games 3 and 4 despite Bryant averaging 33.5 points per game. They won the next two games to advance to the semifinals, then defeated the Spurs in five games to reach the NBA Finals against the Boston Celtics, marking the fifth time in Bryant's career and the first without Shaq that he made the Finals. The Lakers lost to the Celtics in six games. In early September 2008, Bryant decided not to have surgery on his right pinkie. During the 2008–09 season, the Lakers started with a 7–0 record and tied the franchise record for most wins to start the season at 17–2, and by mid-December had a 21–3 record. Bryant was selected to his 11th consecutive All-Star Game as a starter and earned Western Conference Player of the Month for December and January, as well as Western Conference Player of the Week three times. On February 2, 2009, Bryant scored 61 points against the Knicks, setting a record for most points at Madison Square Garden. At the 2009 All-Star Game, he scored 27 points, four assists, four rebounds, and four steals and was named co-MVP with former teammate Shaq. The Lakers finished the regular season with the best record in the West (65–17). Bryant was runner-up in the MVP voting behind James and was selected to the All-NBA First Team and All-Defensive First Team for the seventh time. In the playoffs, the Lakers defeated the Utah Jazz in five games and the Houston Rockets in seven games. They advanced to the Conference Finals by defeating the Denver Nuggets in six games, earning their second straight trip to the NBA Finals. The Lakers defeated the Orlando Magic in five games. Bryant won his first NBA Finals MVP trophy after winning his fourth championship, averaging 32.4 points, 7.4 assists, 5.6 rebounds, 1.4 steals, and 1.4 blocks. He became the first player since West in the 1969 NBA Finals to average at least 32.4 points and 7.4 assists in a Finals series and the first since Jordan to average 30 points, five rebounds, and five assists for a title-winning team. Bryant was the league's leading scorer throughout the 2000s, accumulating 21,065 points in regular season play from 1999–00 to 2008–09. During the 2009–10 season, Bryant made six game-winning shots, including a buzzer-beating, one-legged three-pointer over Dwyane Wade on December 4, 2009, leading to a 108–107 win over the Miami Heat. A week later, Bryant suffered an avulsion fracture in his right index finger in a game against the Minnesota Timberwolves. Despite the injury, he continued playing. Five days after the injury, he made another game-winning shot in overtime against the Milwaukee Bucks. Bryant became the youngest player (31 years, 151 days) to reach 25,000 points, surpassing Chamberlain. He made another game-winning three-pointer against the Sacramento Kings and a game-winning field goal against the Boston Celtics. The following day, he surpassed West to become the all-time leading scorer in Lakers franchise history. After missing five games due to an ankle injury that also caused him to miss the 2010 All-Star Game despite being the Western Conference's leading vote-getter, Bryant returned and made a clutch three-pointer with four seconds remaining against the Memphis Grizzlies. Two weeks later, he made his sixth game-winning shot of the season against the Toronto Raptors. On April 2, 2010, Bryant signed a three-year contract extension worth $87 million. He missed four of the final five games of the regular season due to knee and finger injuries, missing nine games total. The Lakers began the playoffs as the No. 1 seed against the Oklahoma City Thunder, defeating them in six games. They swept the Utah Jazz in the second round and advanced to the Western Conference Finals against the Phoenix Suns. In Game 2, Bryant recorded 13 assists, a playoff career-high, the most by a Laker since Magic Johnson had 13 in 1996. The Lakers won the series in six games to capture the Western Conference Championship and advanced to the NBA Finals for a third straight season. In a rematch against the 2008 champion Boston Celtics, Bryant, despite shooting 6-for-24 from the field, led the Lakers back from a 13-point third-quarter deficit in Game 7 to win the championship. He scored 10 of his 23 points in the fourth quarter and finished with 15 rebounds, tying an NBA Finals record shared by Sam Jones and Tom Gola for rebounds by a shooting guard. Bryant won his fifth championship and earned his second consecutive NBA Finals MVP. This marked the first time the Lakers won a Game 7 against the Celtics in the NBA Finals. Bryant said this was the most satisfying of all his five championships. Bryant wanted a sixth championship to match Jordan's total. The Lakers started the 2010–11 season with eight wins. In his ninth game, against the Denver Nuggets, Bryant became the youngest player in NBA history to reach 26,000 career points. He recorded his first triple-double since January 21, 2009. On January 30, 2011, against the Celtics, Bryant became the youngest player to score 27,000 points. Two days later, he became one of seven players with at least 25,000 points, 5,000 rebounds, and 5,000 assists. On February 10, in a game against the Celtics, Bryant scored 20 of his 23 points in the second half as the Lakers rallied from a 15-point deficit for a 92–86 victory, their first win of the season against a top-four team after entering 0–5 in such matchups and being outscored by an average of 11 points. In the 2011 All-Star Game, Bryant had 37 points, 14 rebounds, and three steals and won his fourth All-Star MVP, tying Hall of Famer Bob Pettit for the most All-Star MVP awards. During the season, Bryant moved from 12th to sixth on the NBA all-time scoring list, passing John Havlicek, Dominique Wilkins, Oscar Robertson, Hakeem Olajuwon, Elvin Hayes, and Moses Malone. Bryant finished the season averaging less than 20 shots per game, his fewest since the 2003–04 season. On April 13, 2011, the NBA fined Bryant $100,000 for directing a gay slur at referee Bennie Adams. The Gay & Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation praised the NBA's decision, and the Human Rights Campaign called the language "disgraceful" and "distasteful." Bryant stated he was open to discussing the matter with gay rights groups and wanted to appeal the fine. He later apologized for using the word. Bryant and other Lakers appeared in a public service announcement denouncing the incident. The Lakers' quest for a three-peat ended when they were swept by the Dallas Mavericks in the second round. Bryant received experimental platelet-rich plasma therapy called Orthokine in Germany to treat pain in his left knee and ankle. Mike Brown replaced the retired Jackson as Lakers coach in the off-season. Bryant began the 2012 season playing with an injured wrist. On January 10, 2012, he scored 48 points against the Suns. "Not bad for the seventh-best player in the league," said Bryant, referring to a preseason ESPN ranking. He scored 40, 42, and 42 in his next three games. This was the sixth time in his career he scored 40 or more points in four straight games, a feat exceeded only by Chamberlain (19 times). At the 2012 All-Star Game, Bryant scored 27 points to pass Jordan as the career scoring leader in the All-Star Game. He also suffered a broken nose and concussion in the third quarter after a hard foul from Dwyane Wade. In April, Bryant missed seven games with a bruised left shin. He returned three games before the end of the regular season and sat out the season finale against Sacramento, foregoing a possible third scoring title as he needed 38 points to surpass Kevin Durant. The Lakers were eliminated in the second round by Durant and Oklahoma City in five games, marking Bryant's final postseason appearance. In 2012–13, the Lakers acquired center Dwight Howard and point guard Steve Nash. On November 2, 2012, Bryant scored 40 points with two steals, passing Magic Johnson (1,724) as the Lakers' career leader in steals. The Lakers lost to the Clippers and started the season 0–3 for the first time in 34 years and only the fourth time in franchise history. After a 1–4 start, coach Brown was fired. He was replaced by Mike D'Antoni, whom Bryant knew from childhood when his father played in Italy and D'Antoni was also a star there. Bryant grew close with D'Antoni during their time with Team USA. On December 5, against New Orleans, Bryant became the youngest player (34 years, 104 days) in league history to score 30,000 points, joining Hall of Famers Chamberlain, Jordan, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, and Karl Malone as the fifth player to reach that milestone. On December 18, in a 101–100 win over the Charlotte Bobcats, Bryant scored 30+ points in his seventh consecutive game, the longest such streak by an NBA player after turning 34; it was the fourth-longest in his career. The streak ended at 10 on December 28 in a 104–87 win over the Portland Trail Blazers when he scored 27 points and sat out the fourth quarter. To improve defense, D'Antoni had Bryant guard the opponent's best perimeter player; he was the primary defender on the Cavaliers' Kyrie Irving, who was held to 15 points. Bryant acknowledged he was a more focused defender after having a challenging assignment compared to playing off the ball against weaker players. His defense disrupted opponents and freed Nash from unfavorable matchups. Bryant led the league in scoring through much of the first 42 games. With a disappointing 17–25 start, D'Antoni had Bryant become the primary facilitator on offense and moved Nash off the ball to become a spot-up shooter. In the next three games, Bryant had at least 10 assists in three wins with a total of 39 assists, the most in his career. He missed a triple-double in each game with nine rebounds twice and eight in the other. In two crucial wins in March, he scored at least 40 points and had at least 10 assists in back-to-back games, becoming the first Laker to do so since West in 1970. Bryant surpassed Chamberlain to become the fourth-leading scorer in league history in a March 30, 2013, victory over Sacramento. With the Lakers fighting to secure the eighth and final playoff berth in the Western Conference and with team injuries, Bryant began playing almost all 48 minutes per game. On April 10, 2013, he became the first player in NBA history to score 47 points, eight rebounds, five assists, four blocks, and three steals in a game. Two days later, Bryant suffered a torn Achilles tendon against the Golden State Warriors, ending his season. The injury occurred while playing seven consecutive quarters and at least 40 minutes for seven consecutive games. The 34-year-old Bryant was averaging his most minutes (38.6) in six years, with only Portland rookie Damian Lillard averaging more. Lakers general manager Mitch Kupchak had discussed the extensive playing time with Bryant 10 days earlier, but Bryant insisted the minutes were necessary due to the playoff push. He had surgery on April 13 to repair the tear and was estimated to miss six to nine months. Bryant ended the season with averages of 27.3 points, 5.6 rebounds, and 6 assists per game on 46.3% shooting. The New York Times called his efforts to bring the Lakers back into playoff contention "perhaps some of the finest work of his career." He reached 40 points eight times during the season and had 10 or more assists in his role as distributor 11 times. He was dubbed "Magic Mamba" after Magic Johnson's passing skills. His assists were the second-highest of his career and his field goal percentage was its highest since 2008–09.

Bryant played in seven consecutive games, averaging his most minutes (38.6) in six years, with only Portland rookie Damian Lillard averaging more. Lakers general manager Mitch Kupchak discussed his playing time with Bryant 10 days earlier, but Bryant insisted the minutes were necessary due to the Lakers' playoff push. He underwent surgery on April 13 to repair a tear, with an estimated absence of six to nine months. Bryant ended the season with averages of 27.3 points, 5.6 rebounds, and 6 assists per game on 46.3% shooting. The New York Times called his leadership in bringing the Lakers back into playoff contention "perhaps some of the finest work of his career." He reached 40 points eight times and had 10 or more assists 11 times in his role as distributor. Bryant was dubbed "Magic Mamba" for his passing skills reminiscent of Magic Johnson. His assists were the second-highest of his career and his field goal percentage was its highest since 2008–09. The Lakers finished the season at 45–37, seventh in the West. Playing without Bryant, they were swept in four games by the San Antonio Spurs in the first round of the playoffs. Bryant resumed practicing in November 2013 after the 2013–14 season began. On November 25, he signed a two-year contract extension with the Lakers valued at $48.5 million, remaining the league's highest-paid player despite accepting a discounted deal, as he was eligible for $32 million per year. The contract sparked debate, with critics arguing stars should earn less to allow team financial flexibility and supporters claiming top stars were underpaid. Bryant returned to play on December 8 after missing the first 19 games, scoring nine points, tying a team-high in assists (eight) and rebounds (four) in a 106–94 home loss to the Toronto Raptors. Nine days later, he matched his season high of 21 points in a 96–92 win over Memphis, but suffered a lateral tibial plateau fracture in his left knee expected to sideline him for six weeks. Bryant had played six games since returning from his Achilles injury, including time at point guard after injuries to Nash, Steve Blake, and Jordan Farmar, averaging 13.8 points, 6.3 assists, and 4.3 rebounds. Despite being sidelined, he was voted by fans to start in his 16th All-Star game, though he felt undeserving and some viewed it as a career achievement award. He missed the game due to knee issues. On March 12, 2014, the Lakers ruled Bryant out for the rest of the season, citing the need for more rehab and limited time remaining; the team was 22–42 and tied for the worst record in the West. The Lakers finished 27–55, missing the playoffs for the first time since 2005. Bryant returned for the 2014–15 season, his 19th with the Lakers, after D'Antoni was replaced by Byron Scott. On November 30, 2014, in a 129–122 overtime win over the Toronto Raptors, Bryant recorded his 20th career triple-double with 31 points, 12 assists, and 11 rebounds. At age 36, he became the oldest NBA player to achieve 30 points, 10 rebounds, and 10 assists in a game. On December 14, he passed Jordan to become the NBA's third all-time leading scorer in a 100–94 victory over Minnesota. Bryant played in the first 27 games of the season, averaging team-highs of 26.4 points and 35.4 minutes per game while leading the league with 22.4 shots per game. Scott held him out for three straight games after a poor performance—nine turnovers, 25 points on 8-for-30 shooting in a 108–101 loss to Sacramento—due to soreness in his knees, feet, back, and Achilles tendons, with Scott planning to reduce Bryant's workload. Bryant exceeded 40 minutes in three games, and the coach blamed himself for overloading Bryant after a strong start. For the season, Bryant shot just 37% from the field and the team went 8–19. In his second game back after resting, he had 23 points, 11 assists, and 11 rebounds in a 111–103 win over Denver, becoming just the third player over 36 to record multiple triple-doubles in a season. On January 21, 2015, Bryant suffered a rotator cuff tear in his right shoulder while driving for a two-handed dunk against the New Orleans Pelicans. Though right-handed, he returned to play, running the offense and shooting, dribbling, and passing with his left hand. Prior to the injury, he had been rested in eight of 16 games. He underwent season-ending surgery, finishing the season averaging 22.3 points but shooting a career-low 37.3%, below his 45.4% career mark. He was expected to miss nine months with a return targeted for the start of the 2015–16 season. The Lakers finished 21–61, surpassing their previous franchise record for most losses in a season. After recovering for the 2015–16 preseason, Bryant suffered a calf injury and missed the final two weeks of exhibition games. He played in the season opener, surpassing John Stockton's record of 19 seasons with one team. On November 24, 2015, the Lakers fell to 2–12 after losing 111–77 to the Warriors; Bryant scored four points in 25 minutes on 1-for-14 shooting, matching his worst-shooting game with at least five attempts. A week later, he played his last game against his hometown team, the Philadelphia 76ers, scoring a team-high 20 points in a 103–91 loss. On November 29, 2015, Bryant announced via The Players' Tribune that he would retire at the end of the season, writing in his poem "Dear Basketball" that he fell in love with the game at age six. In a letter to fans before a game against the Indiana Pacers, he wrote: "What you've done for me is far greater than anything I've done for you. ... My love for this city, this team and for each of you will never fade. Thank you for this incredible journey." At the time of his announcement, Bryant was second on the team in minutes (30.8) behind Jordan Clarkson and led the team with 16.7 field goal attempts per game, averaging just 15.7 points and shooting a career-low 31.5%. His free throw attempts had dropped from his career average, and his game relied heavily on pump fakes and long-range shots, making a league-worst 19.5% from three-point range while attempting seven per game, almost double his career average. In his press conference, Bryant acknowledged his declining skills, stating: "Even though I play like shit, I've worked really, really hard not to play like crap and I do everything I possibly can. And I feel good about that." Bryant requested that opposing teams not hold on-court ceremonies or present public gifts. Prior to retiring, he avoided a staged farewell tour, preferring to hear boos instead of cheers. However, he was honored with video tributes and fan ovations, including at TD Garden, Wells Fargo Center, Moda Center, Sleep Train Arena, and Vivint Smart Home Arena. Previously respected but not beloved, he was astonished by the cheers. On February 3, Bryant made seven three-pointers and scored a season-high 38 points, including 14 of the team's 18 points in the final 5:02, for a 119–115 win over the Minnesota Timberwolves, ending a 10-game losing streak and averting the franchise's longest losing streak. He became just the fourth NBA player over 37 to log at least 35 points, five rebounds, and five assists in a game. He was the leading vote-getter for the 2016 All-Star Game with 1.9 million votes, ahead of Stephen Curry's 1.6 million. Playing as a small forward that season, he was selected as a frontcourt starter for the first time. In his first All-Star game since 2013, he had 10 points, six rebounds, and seven assists. West teammates offered to feed him the ball to earn an All-Star MVP, but he declined. In his final game on April 13, against the Utah Jazz, Bryant scored an NBA season-high 60 points on 50 shots—the most in an NBA game in 30 seasons—outscoring the Jazz 23–21 in the fourth quarter, setting an NBA record for most points in a final regular season game. He became the oldest player to score 60 or more points in a game at 37 years and 234 days old. The Lakers finished the season with a 17–65 record, their worst in franchise history. After the game, he delivered a lengthy speech in front of the Staples Center crowd: "I can't believe how fast 20 years went by... To be standing on the center court with you guys, my teammates behind me, appreciating the journey we've been on—we've been through our ups and downs. The most important part is we all stayed together throughout. Thank you for all the years of support. Thank you for all the motivation. Thank you for all the inspiration. What can I say? Mamba out." Bryant declined to play in the 2000 Olympics due to marrying in the off-season. He also declined to play in the 2002 FIBA World Championship. He was selected for the 2003 FIBA Americas Championship but withdrew after shoulder and knee surgeries. The following summer, he withdrew from the Olympic team due to a sexual assault case. Along with LeBron James, Bryant was one of the first two players named to the 2006–2008 U.S. preliminary roster by Jerry Colangelo, but was sidelined by knee surgery and did not participate in the 2006 FIBA World Championship. Bryant's national team career began in 2007 with the USA Men's Senior National Team and USA FIBA Americas Championship Team, which finished 10–0, won gold, and qualified the U.S. for the 2008 Olympics. He started all 10 games, averaging 15.3 points, 2.9 assists, 2.0 rebounds, and 1.6 steals. On June 23, 2008, he was named to the USA Men's Senior National Team for the 2008 Summer Olympics, his first Olympics. He scored 20 points, including 13 in the fourth quarter, with six assists as Team USA defeated Spain 118–107 in the gold medal game on August 24, 2008, winning its first gold since 2000. He averaged 15.0 points, 2.8 rebounds, and 2.1 assists, shooting .462 from the field in eight games. Bryant rejoined the national team for the 2012 Summer Olympics, winning another gold medal and then retiring from the team. He finished his national team career with a 26–0 record across three tournaments, winning a gold medal each time. Bryant primarily played as a shooting guard, listed at 6 feet 6 inches (1.98 m) and 212 pounds (96 kg), and was often cited as one of the most dangerous scorers in the NBA. He was frequently compared to Michael Jordan, after whom he modeled his style. Like Jordan, he became known for a fall-away jump shot. Chris Ballard of Sports Illustrated described the "jab step-and-pause" as a move where Bryant jabbed his non-pivot foot forward to let the defender relax, then pushed off to drive around the opponent. Bryant also learned post moves from Hakeem Olajuwon. He built a reputation for taking shots in close games, even when double or triple-teamed, and was noted as one of the premier closers. In a 2012 survey of NBA general managers, he was selected for the 10th consecutive season as the player they would want to take a clutch shot. Bryant enjoyed being the villain, reveling in boos and silencing crowds. His shot selection has drawn criticism, with him being labeled a selfish, high-volume shooter; he missed more field goal attempts than any other player in NBA history until LeBron James broke the record in 2024. Phil Jackson noted Bryant "tends to force the action, especially when the game isn't going his way. When his shot is off, Kobe will pound away relentlessly until his luck turns." According to Bryant, "I would go 0 for 30 before I would go 0 for 9; 0 for 9 means you beat yourself, you psyched yourself out of the game." Bryant was also lauded for his defensive skills, rarely drawing charges, which he believed contributed to his longevity. Some critics argue his defensive accolades in later years were based more on reputation than actual play. Bryant was praised for his relentless work ethic, known as the "Mamba mentality." Throughout his first 17 seasons, his body was resilient, and he exhibited a high pain threshold, often playing through injuries. A fierce competitor, he made opponents and teammates alike the objects of his scorn. Many players found him difficult to play with due to his high commitment and performance standards.

Kobe Bryant was known for his relentless work ethic, which he referred to as the "Mamba mentality," and for his ability to go through pain and injuries while maintaining a high level of performance, a trait that contributed to his physical resilience throughout his first 17 seasons. He was a standout defensive player who rarely drew charges, believing this helped preserve his body and extend his career, though some critics argued his later defensive accolades were based more on reputation than actual play. Bryant was described as a fierce competitor who made opponents and teammates feel targeted, and many players found him difficult to play with due to his intense commitment. During the years after Shaquille O'Neal's departure, Bryant led the Lakers to two NBA championships and became more of a mentor to his teammates, with head coach Phil Jackson noting a significant shift in Bryant’s behavior—from demanding the ball to embracing and supporting his teammates personally. Bryant was the youngest of three children, growing up with older sisters Sharia and Shaya, with whom he maintained close relationships. In November 1999, he met 17-year-old Vanessa Laine, who was working as a background dancer on a music video; they began dating and became engaged in May 2000, marrying on April 18, 2001, at St. Edward the Confessor Catholic Church in Dana Point. The marriage was not attended by Bryant’s parents, sisters, agent Arn Tellem, or teammates, as his parents opposed it due to concerns about his age and the race of the woman he was marrying, leading to an estrangement lasting over two years that ended after their first daughter was born. Their first daughter, Natalia, was born in January 2003; Vanessa suffered a miscarriage in 2005 due to an ectopic pregnancy, and their second daughter, Gianna Maria-Onore ("Gigi"), was born in May 2006. Vanessa filed for divorce in December 2011, citing irreconcilable differences, and requested joint custody of their daughters; the divorce was called off on January 11, 2013. Vanessa gave birth to their third daughter in December 2016, and the couple announced in January 2019 they were expecting a fourth daughter, who was born in June 2019. Bryant was a practicing Catholic, and his faith helped him through difficult times, including after the sexual assault allegations; he and his family regularly attended Our Lady Queen of Angels Catholic Church in Newport Beach, and he and Gianna received the Eucharist together just hours before their deaths. He was fluent in English, Italian, and Spanish, and adopted the nickname "Black Mamba" inspired by Uma Thurman’s character in Kill Bill, citing a desire for his basketball skills to mimic the snake’s ability to strike with 99% accuracy at maximum speed in rapid succession. During the 2012–13 season, he began referring to his play as aging like "vino." In January 2002, he purchased a Mediterranean-style house in Newport Coast for $4 million, which he sold in May 2015. In 2013, he had a legal dispute with an auction house over memorabilia from his early years that his parents had put up for sale; the auction house received $450,000, and a settlement allowed them to sell less than 10% of the items, after which Bryant’s parents apologized and acknowledged his financial support. Bryant grew up a fan of baseball, particularly the New York Mets, and had long supported the Los Angeles Dodgers and Angels, though he revealed in 2009 he was a fan of the Mets and still had a Ron Darling card. He was also a lifelong fan of the Philadelphia Eagles and soccer teams Barcelona, AC Milan, and Manchester City. According to Forbes, at retirement, Bryant earned $680 million, the most ever by a team athlete during their playing career. He was a second cousin of Cedric Ceballos, a former Lakers teammate. In summer 2003, Bryant was arrested in Eagle, Colorado, in connection with a sexual assault allegation by a 19-year-old hotel employee; he admitted to an adulterous encounter but denied the assault, and was charged on June 18, 2003. The case was dropped in September 2004 after the accuser declined to testify, and Bryant publicly apologized, acknowledging she did not view the encounter as consensual. The two settled privately. The allegations damaged his reputation, leading to the termination of endorsement deals with McDonald's and Nutella and a significant drop in sales of his replica jerseys. Nike, however, had signed him to a five-year, $40–45 million contract before the incident and refused to use his image or market a new shoe that year, but began promoting him two years later after his image recovered. He resumed endorsement deals with The Coca-Cola Company through Energy Brands for Vitamin Water and appeared on NBA '07: Featuring the Life Vol. 2, Guitar Hero World Tour (with Tony Hawk, Michael Phelps, and Alex Rodriguez), and Call of Duty: Black Ops (with Jimmy Kimmel). In a 2008 Nike Hyperdunk commercial, Bryant appeared jumping over a speeding Aston Martin, a stunt considered fake and possibly a violation of his Lakers contract. After promoting the Hyperdunk, he released the Zoom Kobe IV in 2010, followed by the Zoom Kobe V. In 2009, he signed a deal with Nubeo to market the Black Mamba Collection of luxury watches priced from $25,000 to $285,000. On February 9, 2009, he was featured on the cover of ESPN The Magazine for being a fan of FC Barcelona. CNN estimated his endorsement deals in 2007 at $16 million annually, and in 2010 he was ranked third in Forbes’ list of the world’s highest-paid athletes with $48 million. On December 13, 2010, he signed a two-year deal with Turkish Airlines, appearing in promotional films and advertising across 80 countries. In September 2012, he shot a commercial with FC Barcelona star Lionel Messi, competing to win the attention of a young boy. In 2013, Forbes listed him as the fifth-highest-paid sports star globally, behind Floyd Mayweather, Cristiano Ronaldo, LeBron James, and Lionel Messi. Bryant appeared as the cover athlete for several video games and was a global ambassador for the 2019 FIBA Basketball World Cup in China. In high school, he was part of a rap group called CHEIZAW, named after the Chi Sah gang in Kid with the Golden Arm, which was signed by Sony Entertainment but eventually dropped due to the label’s desire to have Bryant record solo. He performed at a 1997 concert by Sway & King Tech and recorded a verse for a remix of Brian McKnight’s "Hold Me," which peaked at number 35 on the Billboard Hot 100 in January 1999. He also appeared on O'Neal’s Respect, starting the track "3 X's Dope," though his name was not credited. Sony abandoned plans for his debut album, Visions, which was never released, and later dropped him. Afterward, he co-founded Heads High Entertainment, which folded within a year. In 1999, he appeared on a remix of "Say My Name" by Destiny's Child. In 2011, he was featured in Jay Chou’s single "The Heaven and Earth Challenge," with proceeds donated to impoverished schools for basketball facilities and equipment, and the song was used in Sprite’s 2011 China marketing campaign. In 2009, Lil Wayne released a song titled "Kobe Bryant," in 2010 Sho Baraka released "Kobe Bryant On'em," and in 2012 Chief Keef released "Kobe," featured on his debut album. For the NBA 2K21 soundtrack, Damian Lillard released a tribute track titled "Kobe" featuring Snoop Dogg and Derrick Milano. Bryant made his acting debut in 1996 in an episode of Moesha, where he met Brandy, and was her date to her senior prom. He guest-starred in episodes of Arli$$, Sister, Sister, Hang Time, and All That. He was initially chosen for the role of Jesus Shuttlesworth in Spike Lee’s He Got Game but declined, saying "this summer is too big for me." Spike Lee’s 2009 documentary Kobe Doin' Work chronicled Bryant during the 2007–08 NBA season. In 2018, Bryant became the first African-American to win the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film and the first former professional athlete to win an Oscar in any category for his film Dear Basketball, which also won the Annie Award for Best Animated Short Subject and a Sports Emmy Award. The film was produced by his production company, Granity Studios, and he had been in talks with animator Bruce Smith for six months before his death about starting his own animation studio. Beginning in 2018, Bryant wrote, produced, and hosted the television series Detail on ESPN and ESPN+, which featured his insights on basketball and in-depth game analyses. He also appeared on MTV’s Ridiculousness in 2019. Bryant was the official ambassador for After-School All-Stars (ASAS), a nonprofit providing after-school programs in 13 U.S. cities, and co-founded the Kobe Bryant China Fund with the Soong Ching Ling Foundation, which raises funds in China for education and health programs. On November 4, 2010, he appeared alongside Zach Braff at a call.

Kobe Bryant was a prominent figure in basketball, recognized as one of the greatest players in NBA history with career averages of 25.0 points, 5.2 rebounds, 4.7 assists, and 1.4 steals per game. He is the fourth-leading scorer in league history with 33,643 points and the first player to achieve at least 30,000 career points and 6,000 career assists. Bryant led the NBA in scoring during the 2005–06 and 2006–07 seasons, and his 81-point performance against Toronto in 2006 is the second-highest in NBA history, behind only Wilt Chamberlain's 100. He scored at least 50 points 24 times, third in league history behind Jordan (31) and Chamberlain (118), and six times scored at least 60 points. Bryant averaged 40 points in a calendar month four times, the third player in NBA history to do so. He was named the league MVP in 2008 and led the Lakers to the 2008 NBA Finals as the first seed in the Western Conference. Bryant won gold medals at the 2008 and 2012 Summer Olympics, part of the U.S. team known as "The Redeem Team." He won two more championships with the Lakers in 2009 and 2010, earning Finals MVP both times. Bryant was an 18-time All-Star, second only to Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and LeBron James, and was selected a then-record 18 straight times as a starter. He was named All-Star MVP four times, tied with Bob Pettit. Bryant earned 15 All-NBA Team selections, tied with Abdul-Jabbar and Tim Duncan, and 11 first-team honors, tied for second-most with Karl Malone. He was a 12-time All-Defensive Team selection, trailing only Duncan's 15, and named to the All-Defensive First Team nine times, tied with Jordan, Garnett, and Gary Payton. Bryant was the Lakers' all-time leading scorer and tied for the most championships in franchise history with five titles. Both his numbers, 8 and 24, were retired by the Lakers on December 18, 2017. He was named to the NBA 75th Anniversary Team in October 2021 and posthumously inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame in 2021, with Vanessa Bryant delivering the acceptance speech. In 2018, Bryant won an Oscar for Dear Basketball and was also honored with a Sports Emmy Award. He founded the Kobe and Vanessa Bryant Family Foundation, which aims to help young people in need, encourage physical and social skill development through sports, and assist the homeless, emphasizing that homelessness should not be ignored. Bryant was the official ambassador for After-School All-Stars (ASAS), a non-profit providing after-school programs in 13 U.S. cities, and co-founded the Kobe Bryant China Fund, which partners with the Soong Ching Ling Foundation, a Chinese government-backed charity, to raise funds for education and health programs in China. In 2010, Bryant and Zach Braff presented a $1 million check to the Call of Duty Endowment at a launch event in Santa Monica. Bryant established Granity Studios in 2013, which developed films, television shows, and novels, including the Wizenard Series: Training Camp, Legacy and the Queen, Epoca: The Tree of Ecrof, and posthumously released The Wizenard Series: Season One, which topped the New York Times middle-grade hardcover list. Bryant also co-wrote and produced several young adult novels through Granity Studios. Beginning in 2018, he wrote, produced, and hosted the television series Detail on ESPN and ESPN+, featuring insights into basketball and in-depth game analyses. He appeared on MTV's Ridiculousness in 2019. Bryant and his wife founded Kobe Inc., which initially held a 10% stake in Bodyarmor SuperDrink for $6 million in March 2014, with headquarters in Newport Beach, California. After The Coca-Cola Company acquired a minority stake in August 2018, Bryant's stake was valued at approximately $200 million. In 2016, Bryant and business partner Jeff Stibel launched Bryant-Stibel, a venture capital firm with $100 million in funding focused on media, data, gaming, and technology. In 2018, Bryant and Sports Academy launched Mamba Sports Academy, which established locations in Thousand Oaks and Redondo Beach, California, and was later renamed Sports Academy in 2020. On October 23, 2018, Bryant's book The Mamba Mentality, with photographs and an afterword by Andrew D. Bernstein, introduction by Phil Jackson, and foreword by Pau Gasol, was published by MCD / Farrar, Straus and Giroux. At the time of his death, Bryant was working with Brazilian author Paulo Coelho on a children's book for underprivileged children; after his death, Coelho deleted the draft, stating it didn't make sense to publish without him, without specifying the number of pages or title. On January 26, 2020, at 9:06 a.m. Pacific Standard Time, a Sikorsky S-76 helicopter departed from John Wayne Airport with nine people aboard: Bryant, his 13-year-old daughter Gianna, six family friends including John Altobelli, and pilot Ara Zobayan. The helicopter, registered to Island Express Holding Corp., was traveling to Camarillo Airport for a basketball game at Mamba Sports Academy in Thousand Oaks. Due to light rain and fog, Los Angeles Police Department helicopters and most air traffic were grounded. The flight tracker showed the helicopter circling above Glendale due to heavy air traffic. At 9:30 a.m., Zobayan contacted Hollywood Burbank Airport control and was told he was flying too low to be tracked. Amid heavy fog, the helicopter turned south toward the mountains and climbed rapidly from 1,200 to 2,000 feet (370 to 610 meters) at 161 knots (298 km/h; 185 mph). At 9:45 a.m., the helicopter crashed into a mountain in Calabasas, about 30 miles northwest of downtown Los Angeles, beginning to burn. Bryant, his daughter, and the other seven occupants were killed on impact. Initial reports indicated the crash occurred in heavy fog in the hills above Calabasas. Witnesses reported hearing a helicopter struggling before crashing. On January 28, Bryant's identity was confirmed using fingerprints. The Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner-Coroner stated the cause of death for Bryant and the others was blunt force trauma. The Federal Aviation Administration, National Transportation Safety Board, and FBI launched investigations. The NTSB declared on February 9, 2021, that pilot Ara Zobayan probably became disoriented after flying into thick clouds, ignoring his training and violating federal regulations during a 40-minute flight. On February 28, 2023, Vanessa Bryant received a $28.85 million settlement from Los Angeles County to conclude legal proceedings over graphic photos of the crash aftermath shared without family permission, including $15 million from a 2022 civil trial and additional funds for her daughters Natalia, Bianka, and Capri. Chris Chester, a co-plaintiff who lost his wife and daughter in the crash, settled for $19.95 million. On February 7, Bryant and his daughter were buried in a private funeral at Pacific View Memorial Park in Newport Beach, California. A public memorial service was held on February 24 at Staples Center (later Crypto.com Arena), hosted by Jimmy Kimmel, with speakers including Vanessa, Jordan, O'Neal, Diana Taurasi, and Geno Auriemma. The NBA postponed its game against the Clippers on January 28, the first such postponement since the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing. On January 30, the first game at Staples Center after the crash was between the Clippers and Sacramento Kings, with Paul George narrating a tribute to Bryant. The next day, the Lakers played against the Trail Blazers, with a pre-game ceremony featuring Usher singing "Amazing Grace," Boyz II Men singing the national anthem, and Wiz Khalifa and Charlie Puth performing "See You Again" at halftime. James delivered a speech, and every starting player was announced with Bryant's name. The game averaged 4.41 million viewers, the second-most-watched in ESPN history. Beginning with the Spurs and Raptors games on the day of the crash, teams paid tribute with intentional on-court violations referencing Bryant's jersey numbers (24-second shot clock or 8-second backcourt violation). On February 15, NBA commissioner Adam Silver announced the All-Star Game MVP Award would be renamed the NBA All-Star Game Kobe Bryant Most Valuable Player Award. The 62nd Annual Grammy Awards, held on the day of the crash at Staples Center, included tributes, with host Alicia Keys calling the venue "the house that Kobe Bryant built" and joining Boyz II Men in singing "It's So Hard to Say Goodbye to Yesterday." Bryant appeared at the start of the In Memoriam segment of the 92nd Academy Awards following his Oscar win in 2018 for Dear Basketball, with Spike Lee wearing a suit in tribute. He was not included in the montages at the 2020 VMAs and Emmys, which caused fan upset, especially as Naya Rivera and Chadwick Boseman were prominently featured. The 2020 Pro Bowl, played in Orlando on the day of the crash, began with a prayer led by Russell Wilson and included on-field tributes. In the 2020 WNBA draft, Gianna Bryant, Alyssa Altobelli, and Payton Chester were made honorary draft picks. After the Lakers won the 2020 NBA Finals, Snoop Dogg paid homage with a full forearm tattoo. Bryant was posthumously inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame in 2021, with Vanessa delivering the speech. NBA commissioner Adam Silver called Bryant "one of the greatest players in the history of our game," and The New York Times described his career as "one of the most decorated in the history of the sport." Reuters called him "arguably the best player of his generation," and both Sporting News and TNT named him their NBA player of the decade for the 2000s. In 2008 and 2016, ESPN ranked Bryant the second-greatest shooting guard of all time after Michael Jordan. In 2022, The Athletic ranked Bryant the 10th-greatest player in NBA history and the second-highest shooting guard, behind only Jordan. Many peer players, including Kevin Durant, Dirk Nowitzki, Dwyane Wade, and Derrick Rose, called Bryant their generation's version of Jordan. The Press-Enterprise described Bryant as "maybe the greatest Laker in the organization's history." He was the Lakers' all-time leading scorer and tied for the most championships in franchise history. Both his numbers, 8 and 24, were retired by the Lakers on December 18, 2017. Bryant was named a finalist for the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in his first year of eligibility, shortly after his death, and was elected a few months later in April 2020. His formal induction was delayed until 2021 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. In October 2021, Bryant was honored as one of the league's greatest players of all time by being named to the NBA 75th Anniversary Team, which was celebrated during the 2022 NBA All-Star Game in Cleveland, with Bryant receiving one of the loudest cheers of the night.

Kobe Bryant won two more championships in 2009 and 2010, earning the Finals MVP award on both occasions. He was an 18-time All-Star, ranking second behind Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and LeBron James, who each have 19, and he was selected a then-record 18 consecutive times, each as a starter. On four occasions—2003, 2011, 2013, and 2016—he was the leading vote-getter. Bryant was named All-Star MVP four times, sharing the record with Bob Pettit. He was selected to the All-NBA Team 15 times, tied with Abdul-Jabbar and Tim Duncan, and his 11 first-team selections are tied for the second-most with Karl Malone. Bryant was a 12-time All-Defensive Team selection, trailing only Tim Duncan's 15, and earned nine All-Defensive First Team honors, tied with Michael Jordan, Kevin Garnett, and Gary Payton for the most in history. He was the first guard to play 20 seasons in the NBA. Bryant won the NBA Slam Dunk Contest in 1997 and was the youngest winner at the time. Over his career, he scored 40-plus points in 121 games and recorded a triple-double 21 times. During the 2020 NBA playoffs, the Lakers wore 'Black Mamba' jerseys in honor of Bryant, designed by him, featuring a snakeskin pattern with yellow accents and 16 stars representing the team's 16 championships at the time. In a Game 2 victory over the Denver Nuggets in the Western Conference Finals, Anthony Davis made a buzzer-beating three-pointer and yelled Bryant's name while wearing the jerseys. After a Game 2 win in the 2020 NBA Finals, LeBron James said, "It's always special to represent someone that meant so much, not only to the game but also to the Lakers organization for 20-plus years. For us to honor him, being on the floor, this is what it's all about." On January 26, 2022, coinciding with the second anniversary of his death, a statue of Bryant and his daughter Gianna was placed at the crash site in Calabasas. In February, the NBA redesigned the All-Star Game MVP trophy as part of a major redesign of the All-Star Weekend trophies to celebrate the league's 75th anniversary season. On August 24, 2023, on Kobe Bryant Day, the Lakers announced that Bryant's statue outside Crypto.com Arena would be unveiled on February 8, 2024, to honor his two numbers with the Lakers, 8 and 24, and 2 for his daughter Gianna. The statue's inspiration, based on an image of Bryant after his 81-point game pointing a finger toward the sky, was requested by Bryant himself before his death. On August 2, 2024, the Lakers unveiled a statue of Kobe and Gianna Bryant outside Crypto.com Arena. In February 2025, Donald Trump announced that Bryant would receive a statue in the proposed National Garden of American Heroes.
